**Surah Maryam**

Meccan, except for the verse of prostration. It has eight or ninety-nine verses.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad.﴾ Abu 'Amr inclined the *ha'* (*imalah*, the inclination of a vowel toward *i* or *ya'*) because the alifs of the disjointed letters (*asma' al-tahajji*, the names of the letters used as separate sounds) are *ya'*s. Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah inclined the *ya'*, and al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr inclined both of them. Nafi' read in the intermediate manner (*bayn bayn*, between the inclined and the plain vowel). Nafi', Ibn Kathir and 'Asim made the *dal* of *hijaʾ* clear (*izhar*) before the *dhal*, and the rest assimilated it (*idgham*, merging one letter into the next).

﴿The mention of the mercy of your Lord﴾ is the predicate of what precedes it, if the preceding letters are interpreted as referring to the surah or to the Qur'an, since it is contained in it. Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: this that is recited is ﴿the mention of the mercy of your Lord﴾. Or it is the subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning: what is recited to you is the mention of it. It was also read as *dhakara rahmatu* (in the past tense, with *rahmatu* as subject) and as *udhkur* (in the imperative). ﴿His servant﴾ is the object of *al-rahmah* or *al-dhikr*, on the basis that *al-rahmah* is its subject in a figurative extension (*ittisa'*), as in your saying: "The generosity of Zayd reminded me." ﴿Zechariah﴾ is either a substitute (*badal*) for it or an explanatory apposition (*'atf bayan*) to it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 3:

﴿When he called upon his Lord in a secret call.﴾ This is because concealing and speaking aloud are alike before Allah, but concealment is more conducive to humility (ikhbat) and more sincere (ikhlas). Or, lest he be blamed for seeking a child at an advanced age. Or, lest his clients (mawali), whom he feared, should become aware of it. Or, because the weakness of old age made his voice faint. Regarding his age at that time, it is said he was sixty, it is said seventy, it is said seventy-five, it is said eighty-five, and it is said ninety-nine.

﴿My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened within me﴾ explains the call (nida'). Wahn means weakness. The bones are singled out because they are the pillar of the body and the foundation of its structure, and because they are the hardest part of it. When they weaken, what lies beyond them is weaker still. It is stated in the singular because the intended sense is the genus. It has also been read as "wahuna" and "wahina," with damma and kasra, and its counterpart is "kamula," which is read with all three vowels.

﴿and the head has blazed with white hair﴾. He likened the whiteness and brightness of the grey hair to the flame of fire, and its spreading and pervasion through the hair to the spreading of fire. Then he expressed this in the form of a metaphor (isti'ara) and attributed the blazing to the head, which is the place of the grey hair, for emphasis. He made the word "shayban" a specifier (tamyiz) to clarify the intended meaning. He used the definite article "al-" in place of an possessive construction, to indicate that the addressee's knowledge of the specific intended meaning makes the restriction unnecessary.

﴿And I have never been unblessed in my supplication to You, my Lord﴾. Rather, every time I called upon You, You responded to me. This is a means of seeking nearness (tawassul) through what preceded with it of response, and an indication that although the one prayed for is not customary, granting it is customary. He, exalted is He, accustomed him to answer and made him hope for it. It is the right of the generous that he not disappoint one whom he has made hopeful.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 5–6:

﴿And indeed I fear the mawali (my kinsmen) after me﴾. He means the sons of his paternal uncle, and they were among the worst of the Children of Israel. So he feared that they would not manage his succession over his community well, and would alter their religion for them (p-6)

﴿from behind me﴾ after my death. It is also related from Ibn Kathir, with the mad and the qasr and with a fatha on the ya', that it is connected to an omitted element, or it has the meaning of the mawali, i.e., I feared the conduct of the mawali from behind me, or those who will take charge of the matter from behind me. It has been recited as "khiftu al-wali min waraii", meaning: they will be few and unable to establish the religion after me, or they will be weak and será ahead of me, and on this reading the adverbial phrase is connected to "khiftu". ﴿And my wife has been barren﴾, unable to bear children. ﴿So grant me from Yourself﴾, for such a thing is not hoped for except from Your bounty and the perfection of Your power, since I and my wife are not fit for childbearing. ﴿an heir﴾ from my own loins.

﴿who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub﴾: two attributes of him. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i apocopated both, considering them the answer to the supplication. What is intended is the inheritance of the Law and of knowledge, for the prophets do not bequeath wealth. It has been said that he inherits from me the rabbinate (al-Hubura), for he was a rabbi (habr), and inherits from the family of Ya'qub the kingship, and Ya'qub here is the son of Ishaq, upon both of them be prayers and peace. It has also been said that Ya'qub was the brother of Zakariyya, or of 'Imran ibn Mathan, from the offspring of Sulayman, upon him be peace. It has been recited as "yarithuni wa-arith al-i Ya'qub" as a circumstantial (hal) construction from one of the two pronouns; and "Uwayrith" in the diminutive, because of his youth; and "warithun min al-i Ya'qub" as the subject of "yarithuni". This is called at-tajrid in the science of rhetoric, because he was stripped of the one first mentioned while being intended.

﴿And make him, my Lord, one with whom You are pleased﴾: pleasing to You in word and deed.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 7:

﴿O Zakariyya, indeed We give you good news of a boy whose name is Yahya﴾ This is an answer to his call and a promise that his supplication will be granted. The naming was assigned directly to Allah only as an honour to him (tashrif).

﴿We have not made for him before, any namesake﴾ No one was named Yahya before him. This is evidence that giving unfamiliar names is a way of elevating the one named. It is also said that "namesake" (samiyy) means "equal," as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do you know anyone worthy of the same name as Him?﴾, because two alike share a name. The more apparent view is that the name is non-Arabic (a'jami); and if it is Arabic, it is derived from a verb, like "he lives" (ya'ish) and "he prospers" (ya'mur). It is also said that he was named this because the womb of his mother came to life through him, or because the religion of Allah came to life through his call.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verses 8–9:

﴿He said, "My Lord, how can I have a son when my wife is barren and I have reached extreme old age, decrepitude?"﴾ *ʿitiyyan* means stiffness and dryness in the joints. Its root is *ʿutuww*, on the pattern of *quʿūd*. They found the succession of the two *ḍamma*s and the two *wāws* heavy, so they changed the *tāʾ* to a *kasra*. The first *wāw* was then changed to a *yāʾ*, and then the second was changed and assimilated. Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafṣ read *ʿitiyyan* with a *kasra* (on the *ʿayn*). Zechariah was only astonished at having a child, an aged old man and a barren old woman, as an acknowledgement that the one who brings it about is the perfection of God's power, and that intermediaries, on close examination, count for nothing. For this reason, ﴿He said﴾, that is, God Most High, or the angel who conveyed the good news, confirming him. ﴿Thus﴾, that is, the matter is so. The *kāf* may also be in the accusative governed by ﴿He said﴾ in ﴿Your Lord said﴾, and *dhālika* (thus) then refers to something vague which the following clause explains. ﴿It is easy for Me﴾. The first reading is supported by the reading of whoever read *wa-huwa ʿalayya hayyin* (and it is easy for Me): the matter is as I said, or as I promised, and on that basis it is easy for Me. Or: as I promised, and it is easy for Me; I do not need, in what I wish to do, to rely on causes. The second object of *qāla* is omitted. ﴿And I created you before, when you were nothing﴾: rather, you were utterly non-existent. This contains evidence that the non-existent is not a thing. Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read *wa-qad khalaqnāka* (We created you).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verses 10–11:

﴿He said: "My Lord, appoint for me a sign."﴾ A sign, a marker by which I may know the occurrence of what You have given me good news of. ﴿He said: "Your sign is that you shall not speak to people for three nights, while sound."﴾ Sound in form (sawiyy al-khalq), with no muteness or dumbness in you. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 16:

﴿And mention in the Book﴾ — in the Qur'an. ﴿Maryam﴾ — meaning her story. ﴿When she withdrew﴾ — she secluded herself. It is a substitute (badal) for "Maryam": a badal al-ishtimal (substitution of inclusion), since times include what occurs within them; or a badal al-kull (substitution of the whole), since what is meant by "Maryam" is her story, and by the time-phrase the event that occurred in it, and these two are one. Or it is an adverbial complement (zarf) of an assumed governing noun (mudaf muqaddar). It has also been said that ﴿idh﴾ here carries the meaning of the verbal particle "an" (that), as in your saying, "I honored you because you did not honor me," in which case it is necessarily a substitute. ﴿From her family, to a place toward the east﴾ — east of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), or east of her house. For this reason the Christians took the east as their qibla. "Makanan" is either an adverbial complement (zarf) or an object (maf'ul), since ﴿intabadhat﴾ (she withdrew) implicitly carries the meaning of ﴿atat﴾ (she came to).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 17:

﴿So she took a screen apart from them﴾, a curtain. ﴿Then We sent to her Our Spirit, and it appeared to her as a man in every respect.﴾ It is said that she sat in a recess (mishraqah) for ghusl from menstruation, screened by something that covered her. Whenever she menstruated, she would move from the mosque to the house of her maternal aunt, and return to it when she became pure. So while she was in her place of bathing, Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to her, appearing in the form of a beardless young man of well-formed build, so that she would be at ease with his speech. Perhaps it was to stir her desire through him, so that his seed would descend into her womb.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 18–19:

﴿She said: "Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you."﴾ From the utmost of her chastity. ﴿If you are God-fearing﴾ — fearing God and taking seriously the seeking of refuge. The apodosis of the conditional is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, meaning: "Then indeed I am seeking refuge from you," or "then you will be admonished by my seeking refuge," or "then do not approach me." It is also permissible that it is for emphasis, meaning: "If you are God-fearing and scrupulous, then indeed I seek refuge from you," so how much more so if you are not like that.

﴿He said: "I am only the messenger of your Lord"﴾ — the One by whom you sought refuge. ﴿to give you a pure boy﴾ — meaning, that I may be the cause of his being given by breathing into the garment (al-dir', the shirt). It is also permissible that this is a narration of the saying of God Most High, and it is supported by the recitation of Abu 'Amr, and most narrators from Nafi' and Ya'qub, with the yā' (﴿لِيَهَبَ﴾ "that He may give").

﴿pure﴾ — free from sins, or growing upon goodness, meaning progressing from one stage of age to another upon goodness and righteousness.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verses 20–21:

﴿She said: "How can I have a boy when no man has touched me?"﴾ That is, no man has lawfully had intercourse with me. These expressions (al-kinayat) are used only of marriage, whereas for illicit intercourse (al-zina) one says "she was corrupt with it" (khabutha biha), "she committed immorality" (fajara), and the like. This is reinforced by the conjunction with her words: ﴿and I have not been unchaste﴾ (baghiyyan), which is connected to it (ʿalayhi). Baghiyy is on the pattern fa'ul, from al-baghy (transgression). Its waw was changed into a ya', the two were assimilated (idgham), and then the ghayn was kasra'd for harmony (ittiba'an). For this reason the taʾ marbuta (tâʾ) is not attached to it. Or it is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of fa'il (active), and the tâʾ is not attached to it because it expresses intensity (lil-mubalagha). Or it is for the relative sense (lil-nasab), like ṭāliq (having divorced, i.e., one related to divorce).

﴿He said: "So it is; your Lord said: 'It is easy for Me, and that We may make him﴾ That is, "We will do that so that We may make him a sign," or "so that We may show through it Our power," and "that We may make him." It was said that it is conjoined (ʿutifa) to "li-yahaba" (that He may bestow) in the manner of iltifat (shift of grammatical person). ﴿a sign for mankind﴾, a mark for them and a proof of the perfection of Our power. ﴿and a mercy from Us﴾ upon the servants, by which they are guided through his instruction. ﴿And it was a matter decreed﴾ That is, the decree of God in eternity was attached to it, or it was determined and inscribed in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh), or it was a matter worthy of being decreed and done because of its being a sign and a mercy.

Or it is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of fa'il (active), and the tâʾ is not attached to it because it expresses intensity (lil-mubalagha). Or it is for the relative sense (lil-nasab), like ṭāliq (having divorced, i.e., one related to divorce).

﴿He said: "So it is; your Lord said: 'It is easy for Me, and that We may make him﴾ That is, "We will do that so that We may make him a sign," or "so that We may show through it Our power," and "that We may make him." It was said that it is conjoined (ʿutifa) to "li-yahaba" (that He may bestow) in the manner of iltifat (shift of grammatical person). ﴿a sign for mankind﴾, a mark for them and a proof of the perfection of Our power. ﴿and a mercy from Us﴾ upon the servants, by which they are guided through his instruction. ﴿And it was a matter decreed﴾ That is, the decree of God in eternity was attached to it, or it was determined and inscribed in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh), or it was a matter worthy of being decreed and done because of its being a sign and a mercy.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 19, verse 22:**

﴿So she conceived him﴾, by blowing into the opening of her garment, so the breath entered her womb. The period of her pregnancy was seven months. It is also said six, and it is said eight. No child born after eight months has survived except him. It is also said that it was an hour, as she carried him she cast him off. Her age was thirteen years, and it is said ten years, and she had menstruated twice. ﴿And she withdrew with him﴾, that is, she secluded herself while he was in her womb, as in his saying:

*"You trample upon us the skulls and the dust."*

The prepositional phrase (*al-jarr wal-majrur*) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*). ﴿To a remote place﴾, far from her people, behind the mountain. It is also said, to the farthest part of the house.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 23:

﴿So the pains of childbirth drove her﴾ — fa- alja'ahā (drove her, compelled her) al-makhāḍ (the pains of labour), which in origin is transferred from jā'a (to come), but it was specialised in usage, like ātā in a'ṭā (to give). It is also recited al-mikhāḍ with a kasra, and both are a verbal noun of makhadati al-mar'atu (the woman's labour pains began), when the child moves in her womb for coming out.

﴿to the trunk of the palm tree﴾ so that she might conceal herself behind it and lean on it at the time of birth. It is what lies between the root and the branch. It was a dry palm with no crown and no greenery, and the time was winter. The definite article is either generic (lil-jins) or for a known referent (lil-'ahd), since there was no other palm there, and it was well known among people. Perhaps God, exalted is He, inspired her with this so that He might show her among His signs what would calm her fright and feed her with fresh dates (rutab), which is the postpartum remedy suited to her.

﴿She said: "Would that I had died before this"﴾ out of shame before people and fear of their blame. Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr recited ﴿mittu﴾ from màta yamūtu (to die).

﴿and I had been a thing forgotten﴾ something that should be forgotten and not sought; its parallel is al-dhabḥ (the slaughtered animal) for that which is slaughtered. Hamza and Hafs recited with a fatḥa, and it is a dialect form of it, or a verbal noun named as such. It was also recited with that and with hamz, meaning the milk mixed with water which its people discard (yanssa'uhu) because of its scarcity.

﴿forgotten﴾ utterly forgotten, such that it does not occur to their minds. It was also recited with a kasra on the mīm by way of imitation (ittibā').

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 24:

﴿Then [he/it] called to her from beneath her﴾ [i.e., the infant, ʿĪsā], and it is said [it was] Jibril (Gabriel); he used to receive the child. It is also said that "beneath her" means lower than her place. Nafiʿ, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Ḥafs and Rawḥ read ﴿min taḥtihā﴾ with a kasra and a jarr [i.e., as min taḥtihi, "from beneath him"], on the basis that in nādā (he called) there is a pronoun referring to one of them [i.e., to the one calling, Jibril or ʿĪsā]. It is also said that the pronoun in taḥtihā refers to the palm tree. (p-9)

﴿Do not grieve﴾, i.e., do not grieve, or [it is read as] "that you should not grieve." ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream (sarīyan)﴾, i.e., a rivulet. This is how it is narrated in the marfūʿ form. It is also said that sarīyan means a master (sayyid), derived from al-sarw (nobility), and that this is ʿĪsā, upon whom be peace.

﴿And shake towards you the trunk of the palm tree﴾. "Towards you" means: bend it toward yourself. The preposition *bi* (the "ba'") in *bi-jidh'i* is extra (*zā'idah*), added for emphasis. Alternatively, the verb is to be read as an instruction to perform the shaking and bending with it. Or the meaning is: shake the fruit by means of shaking the trunk. *Al-hazz* (shaking) is moving something by pulling and pushing.

﴿It will drop upon you﴾: the original is *tatasāqaṭu*, "it will drop," with the second *tā'* assimilated into the *sīn* (*idghām*, consonant assimilation). Ḥamzah deleted it. Yaʿqūb read it with *yā'*, and Ḥafṣ read *tusāqiṭ* from *sāqaṭat*, meaning *asqaṭat* (it caused to fall). It is also recited as *tatasāqaṭ*, *tasquṭ* and *yasquṭ*. The *tā'* refers to the palm tree and the *yā'* refers to the trunk.

﴿fresh ripe dates﴾: *ruṭaban* is either a specification (*tamyīz*) or an object. It is reported that it was a dry palm tree with no top and no fruit, and it was winter. She shook it, and God the Exalted gave it a top, fronds and ripe dates.

The purpose of her consolation through this is the miracles it contains, which indicate the innocence of her honour, for such a thing cannot be conceived of someone who commits indecencies. It also serves as a reminder to whoever sees it that the One who can make a dry palm bear fruit in winter can make her conceive without a male, and that this is not strange in her case, together with the drink and food it contains. For this reason He arranged the two matters upon it, saying:

**So eat and drink.** That is, from the dates and the water of the stream, or from the dates and their juice. **"And let your eye be refreshed."** Be content in yourself and cast off whatever grieves you. It is also recited as «وَقِرى» (*waqiri*) with a kasra, and this is the dialect of Najd. Its derivation is from *al-qarar* (settling): when the eye sees what gladdens the soul, it settles upon it rather than looking at other things. Or it derives from *al-qurr* (coolness): the tear of joy is cool and the tear of grief is hot. For this reason one says *qurrat al-ayn* (coolness of the eye) of the beloved, and *sakhanat al-ayn* (heat of the eye) of the disliked.

**"And if you see any human being..."** that is, if you see a human. It is also recited as «تَرَئِنَّ» (*tara'inna*), according to the dialect of those who say «لَبَأْتُ بِالحَجِّ» (*labba'tu bil-hajj*), owing to the interchange between the hamza and the soft letter.

**"Then say, 'Indeed I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast.'"** meaning silence (*samt*), and it has been recited with that reading; or fasting (*siyam*), for they did not speak during their fasts.

**"So I will not speak today to any human being."** after having told you of my vow. I will only speak with the angels and converse with my Lord.

It was said that she informed them of her vow by gesture, and he commanded her to do so, because of his dislike of argument and to suffice with the speech of Jesus, peace be upon him, for it is decisive in silencing the accuser.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 27–28:

﴿Then she brought him﴾, i.e., with her child, ﴿to her people﴾, returning to them after she had become clean from postnatal bleeding (nifas), ﴿carrying him﴾, bearing him. ﴿They said: O Maryam, you have certainly come with a thing unprecedented﴾, i.e., something wondrous and abominable, from the verb farā al-jild (the skin was split open).

﴿O sister of Harun﴾. They meant Harun the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, and she was from the descendants of one who was among his contemporaries in the generation of brotherhood. It is said she was from his offspring, and there were a thousand years between them. It is also said that he was a righteous or wicked man who lived in their time, and they likened her to him in mockery, or because of the righteousness they had seen in her before, or they insulted her with it. ﴿Your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother an unchaste woman﴾: this is an affirmation that what she brought is a fabrication (fariy), and an alert that the grave sins of the children of the righteous are more heinous.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on Surah 19, verses 29–30:

﴿So she pointed to him.﴾ That is, to ʿIsā (peace be upon him). I.e., "Speak to him so that he may answer you." ﴿They said, "How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?"﴾ We had not known of a child in the cradle who spoke to an intelligent person. Here *kāna* (كانَ) is *zāʾidah* (redundant, i.e., an extra particle with no independent meaning), and the adverbial phrase *fī al-mahd* (في المَهْدِ) is the *ṣilah* (the relative clause) of *man* (مَن). *Ṣabiyyan* (صَبِيًّا) is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative) from the pronoun hidden in it. Alternatively, *kāna* is *tāmmah* (complete, meaning "existed"), or *dāʾimah* (continuous), as in His saying, ﴿And Allah has always been Knowing and Wise﴾, or it means *ṣāra* (became).

﴿He said, "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah."﴾ Allah Most High made him speak these words first, because it is the first of the *maqāmāt* (stations, i.e., stages of the prophetic mission), and as a refutation of those who claim his lordship (*rubūbiyyah*). ﴿He has given me the Book﴾, that is, the Injīl (Gospel). ﴿And made me a prophet.﴾

﴿That is Jesus, son of Mary﴾ — that is, the one whose description has preceded: he is Jesus, son of Mary, not what the Christians describe. Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on Surah 19, verses 35–36:

﴿It is not befitting for God to take a son. Glory be to Him.﴾ This is a refutation of the Christians and a declaration of God's transcendence above what they have slandered Him with. ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ This is a rebuke to them, for whoever, when He wills a thing, brings it into existence with ﴿Be﴾ is exalted above resemblance to created beings, who need to take a son through the impregnation of females. Ibn ʿĀmir read ﴿فَيَكُونُ﴾ (fa-yakūnu) with a fatḥa (naṣb, the accusative/subjunctive mood) as a response (jawāb, the clause that answers a conditional) to the preceding clause.

﴿And indeed God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path.﴾ Its interpretation has already been given in the Surah of Āl ʿImrān. The two Hijazi readers and the two Basran readers read ﴿وأنَّ﴾ (wa-anna) with a fatḥa, as "wa-li-anna" (and because). It has also been said that it is coordinated (maʿṭūf) with ﴿بِالصَّلاةِ﴾ (bi-l-ṣalāh, "with prayer") in the preceding verse.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 37:

﴿So the factions differed among themselves﴾ — the Jews and the Christians, or the sects of the Christians: the Nestorians (Nasturiyya), who said, "He is the son of God"; (p-11)

and the Jacobites (Ya'qubiyya), who said, "He is God, who descended to the earth and then ascended to the heaven"; and the Melkites (Malkaniyya), who said, "He is the servant of God and His prophet." ﴿So woe to those who disbelieved because of the scene of a great day﴾ — "the scene" (mashhad) of a great day means its witnessing (shuhud): its terror, its reckoning and its recompense. This is the Day of Resurrection. Or it means "from the time of witnessing," or "from its place therein." Or it means the testimony of that day against them, which is that the angels, the prophets, their tongues, their hands and their feet will testify against them for their disbelief and their transgression. Or it means "from the time of testimony" or "from its place." It has also been said that it refers to what they testified concerning Jesus and his mother.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 38:

﴿How well they will hear and see on the Day they come to Us!﴾ This is an expression of wonder (taʿajjub); its meaning is that their hearing and their sight are [deserving of wonder]. ﴿On the Day they come to Us﴾, i.e., the Day of Resurrection, is worthy of their hearing and seeing being marvelled at, after they were deaf and blind in the world. Or it is a threat: [they will hear and see] what they will hear and see on that Day. It has also been said that [God] commanded him to make them hear and see the promises of that Day and what will befall them therein. The prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa'l-majrur) is in the nominative position according to the first reading and in the accusative position according to the second. ﴿But the wrongdoers today are in manifest error.﴾ He placed "the wrongdoers" in the position of the pronoun, indicating that they wronged themselves in that they neglected hearing and looking at the time when it would have benefited them, and he recorded their neglect as being "manifest error."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 39–40:

﴿And warn them of the Day of Regret⁠﴾ — the Day when people will regret, the wrongdoer over his wrongdoing and the doer of good over how little of his good he did. ﴿When the matter has been decided⁠﴾ — meaning, when the reckoning has been concluded and the two groups have been separated, one to Paradise and the other to the Fire. Here "idh" (when) is either a substitute (badal) for "the Day" or an adverbial complement (zarf) governed by ﴿the Regret⁠﴾. ﴿While they are heedless and do not believe⁠﴾ — this is a circumstantial clause (hal) related to the statement ﴿in manifest error⁠﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD). Alternatively, it is related to ﴿warn them⁠﴾, meaning: warn them while they are heedless and unbelieving, so that the circumstantial clause carries the sense of causation (ta'lil).

﴿Indeed, We shall inherit the earth and whoever is upon it⁠﴾ — none will remain upon it other than Us; there will be no owner or possessor of it apart from Us. Or it means: We shall cause the earth and whoever is upon it to pass away through annihilation and destruction, just as an heir passes away upon inheriting. ﴿And to Us they will be returned⁠﴾ — they will be sent back for recompense.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verses 41–42:

﴿And mention in the Book Abraham; indeed he was a man of truth﴾: constantly adhering to truthfulness, or one who affirmed the truth very much, because of his great affirmation of the unseen matters of God, the Exalted, and His signs, books and messengers. ﴿A prophet﴾: whom God informed (of revelation) (istanba'ahu Allah).

﴿When he said﴾ is a substitution (badal, apposition) for Abraham, and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD), or it is connected to ﴿was﴾ or to ﴿a man of truth, a prophet﴾. ﴿To his father: O my father﴾: the taa' (in yā abatī) is a replacement for the yā' of possession (yā' al-idafa), and for this reason one does not say yā abatī but says yā abatā. It is mentioned to evoke compassion, and for this reason he repeated it. ﴿Why do you worship what does not hear and does not see﴾, so that it knows your condition, hears your call and sees your submission. ﴿And does not avail you anything﴾ in bringing about a benefit or repelling a harm. How much more so when it is an inanimate object that neither hears nor sees. So he said: (p-12)

Translation of the passage:

﴿O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so you become a companion to Satan﴾ (walīyan): a companion in the curse and the punishment, [who] follows him and he follows you; or one who is steadfast in allegiance to him, for it (the punishment) is greater than the punishment, just as the good pleasure of Allah is greater than the reward. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 46:

﴿Said he: "Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham?"﴾ He met his (Abraham's) gentleness and his kindness in guidance with harshness and the severity of obstinacy. So he called him by his name and did not answer "O my father" with "O my son." He delayed (the vocative) and put the predicate before the subject, and he opened with the interrogative hamza (alif) to denounce the very act of turning away, in a kind of wonder, as if it were something no rational person would turn away from. Then he threatened him, saying: ﴿"If you do not desist"﴾ from your speech about them, or from turning away from them. ﴿"I will surely stone you"﴾ with my tongue, meaning with abuse and blame, or with stones until you die, or (until) you keep away from me. ﴿"And leave me alone"﴾ is coordinated with what is indicated by ﴿"I will surely stone you"﴾, i.e., beware of me and leave me alone. ﴿"For a long time"﴾ means a long period of time, from al-mala' (long duration), or "for a long time" in going away from me.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verses 47–48:

﴿He said: "Peace be upon you."﴾ It is a farewell, a parting, and a repaying of evil with good; that is, "I will not inflict upon you anything disliked, nor will I say to you anything that would hurt you hereafter. But: ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾, perhaps He will grant you success in repentance and faith. For the true meaning of seeking forgiveness for an unbeliever is requesting that success be granted to him in that which necessitates his forgiveness, and its explanation has already passed in Surat al-Tawbah." ﴿Indeed, He has been ever gracious to me﴾, meaning, exceedingly kind and gentle in His favour.

﴿And I will withdraw from you and what you invoke besides Allah﴾, by migrating for the sake of my religion. ﴿And I will call upon my Lord﴾, worshipping Him alone. ﴿Perhaps I shall not be in my supplication to my Lord unfortunate﴾, that is, disappointed, with my effort wasted, like you in your supplication to your gods. The opening of the statement with ﴿perhaps (ʿasā)﴾ expresses humility and self-abasement, and draws attention to the fact that answering and rewarding are a bounty, not two things that are obligatory, and that the determining factor of the matter is its outcome, which is unseen.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 49–50:

﴿So when he separated himself from them and from what they worshipped besides Allah﴾ by emigrating to al-Sham (Syria). ﴿We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾ in place of those among the disbelievers from whom he had parted. It is said that when he set out for al-Sham, he first came to Harran, married Sarah, and she bore him Isaac, and from him was born Jacob. Perhaps their being singled out for mention is because they are the two trees of the prophets (ashjar al-anbiya'), or because he wished to remind Isma'il of his (Allah's) favour upon him individually. ﴿And each We made a prophet﴾, each of them or of them (all).

﴿And We bestowed upon them of Our mercy﴾: prophethood, wealth and children. ﴿And We granted them a tongue of truthfulness, sublime﴾: people take pride in them and praise them, in response to his supplication ﴿And grant me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations﴾. By "tongue" is meant that by which speech is conveyed; the "tongue of the Arabs" is their language. Its being attributed to truthfulness and described as sublime indicates that they are deserving of the praise they receive, and that their virtues remain unconcealed despite the distance of eras, the shifting of dynasties and the changing of religions.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verses 51–53:

﴿And mention in the Book Moses; indeed he was sincere (mukhlaṣan)﴾: a monotheist who made his worship sincere, free from association (shirk) and showing-off (riya’). Or, he submitted his face to God and made his self sincere, devoted to Him alone, free from anything other than Him. The Kufans read it with a fatha (mukhlaṣan), meaning that God had made him sincere. ﴿And he was a messenger (rasūl), a prophet (nabī)﴾: God sent him to the creation, and he informed them of Him. For this reason he mentioned "messenger" before "sincere," although sincerity is more exalted.

﴿And We called him from the right side of the Mount (al-Ṭūr)﴾: from its right-hand side, which is the side nearest to Moses's right hand, from the blessed side toward Yemen, in that speech was presented to him from that direction. ﴿And We brought him near﴾: a bringing near of honour, which likened him to one whom a king brings near for private conversation. ﴿Confidentially (najiyyan)﴾: conversing in private, a state (ḥāl) of one of the two pronouns. It was also said: raised up, from al-najwah, which means elevation, because it is reported that he was raised above the heavens until he heard the scratching of the Pen.

﴿And We granted him, out of Our mercy﴾: out of Our mercy, or some of Our mercy. ﴿His brother﴾: the support of his brother and his aid was a response to his supplication. ﴿And appoint for me a minister from my family﴾: he was older than Moses. It is an object (maf‘ūl) or a substitute (badal), on the assumption that "min" is partitive (lil-tab‘īḍ). ﴿Aaron (Hārūn)﴾: an explanatory appositive (ʿaṭf bayān) for him. ﴿A prophet (nabiyyan)﴾: a state (ḥāl) of him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 58:

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to those mentioned in the surah, from Zakariyya to Idris, upon them be peace. ﴿upon whom Allah bestowed favour﴾ with kinds of blessings, religious and worldly, ﴿of the prophets﴾ is an explanation of the relative pronoun. ﴿of the offspring of Adam﴾ is a substitute for it, with the preposition repeated. It is also permissible that ﴿of﴾ here be partitive, because those upon whom favour was bestowed are more general than the prophets and more specific than the offspring. ﴿And of those whom We carried with Noah﴾, meaning and of the offspring of those whom We carried, specifically, and they are all except Idris, for Abraham was of the offspring of Sam son of Noah. ﴿And of the offspring of Abraham﴾, the rest. ﴿And Israel﴾ is conjoined to Abraham, meaning and of the offspring of Israel, and among them were Musa, Harun, Zakariyya, Yahya and Isa, and in this is evidence that the children of daughters are counted among the offspring. ﴿And of those whom We guided﴾, and among those whom We guided to the truth. ﴿And chose﴾ for prophethood and honour. ﴿When the signs of the Most Merciful were recited to them, they fell down prostrating and weeping﴾ is the predicate of ﴿those﴾ if you make the relative pronoun its attribute, and it is a resumed statement if you make it the predicate, to explain their fear of Allah and their humility before Him, along with their high rank in nobility of lineage, perfection of soul, and nearness to Allah, exalted is He.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ), upon him be prayer and peace: "Recite the Qur'an and weep; and if you do not weep, then feign weeping."

And ﴿bukiyyan﴾ is the plural of "baki" (weeping one), like "sujud" is the plural of "sajid". It has been read ﴿yutla﴾ with a ya', because the feminine here is not real. And Hamzah and al-Kisai read ﴿bikiyyan﴾ with a kasra on the ba'.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 59:

﴿Then there succeeded them a later generation﴾, meaning their offspring (ʿaqib), and there came after them a bad posterity (ʿaqib suʾ). It is said: khalaf ṣidq (with a fatḥa on the lam, meaning a good successor) and khalf suʾ (with a sukun on the lam, meaning a bad successor). ﴿They neglected the prayer﴾: they abandoned it or delayed it beyond its time. ﴿And followed their desires﴾: such as drinking wine, deeming marriage to a paternal half-sister lawful, and immersing themselves in acts of disobedience.

It is related from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning His words ﴿and followed their desires﴾: [they were of] the building of the lofty (shadid), the riding of the ornamented (manzur), and the wearing of the renowned (mashhur). ﴿So they will meet with Ghayy﴾: evil, as in his saying:

Whoever meets good, people will praise his conduct... and whoever goes astray will not lack a blamer for his error

Or it means the recompense of ghayy, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿they will meet with sin (atham)﴾. Or ghayy means straying from the path of Paradise. It is said that it is a valley in Hell from which its valleys seek refuge.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verses 60–61:

﴿Except for one who repents, believes, and does righteous deeds﴾ indicates that the verse concerns the disbelievers. ﴿Then those will enter Paradise﴾ Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr and Ya'qub read it in the passive voice from adkhala (causing to enter). ﴿And they will not be wronged in anything﴾ meaning they will not be deprived of anything of the reward of their deeds. The word ﴿shay'an﴾ may be parsed as an accusative of the verbal noun (maf'ul mutlaq, absolute object), and this carries an indication that their previous disbelief will not harm them nor diminish their rewards.

﴿Gardens of perpetual residence (jannat 'adn)﴾ is a substitution (badal al-ba'd, partial substitution) for "Paradise," since it comprises them. Alternatively, it is in the accusative as an expression of praise (al-mad'h). It is also read in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject. ﴿'Adn﴾ is treated as a proper noun because it is the thing added to (al-mudaf ilayhi) in the sense of a proper name, or it is a proper name for "residence" (al-'adn bi-ma'na al-iqamah), like Burrah. For this reason it is valid to describe what is annexed to it by the phrase ﴿which the Most Merciful has promised to His servants in the unseen﴾, meaning He promised them while they are absent from it, or while they are absent from it (the gardens), or He promised them for their faith in the unseen.

﴿Indeed He﴾ i.e., Allah. ﴿His promise﴾ which is Paradise. ﴿is ever fulfilled (ma'tiyyan)﴾ its people will come to it, those promised to them, without doubt. It is said that it derives from "ata ilayhi ihsanan," meaning an accomplished, fulfilled favor.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verses 60–61:

﴿Except for one who repents, believes, and does righteous deeds﴾ indicates that the verse concerns the disbelievers. ﴿Then those will enter Paradise﴾ Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr and Ya'qub read it in the passive voice from adkhala (causing to enter). ﴿And they will not be wronged in anything﴾ meaning they will not be deprived of anything of the reward of their deeds. The word ﴿shay'an﴾ may be parsed as an accusative of the verbal noun (maf'ul mutlaq, absolute object), and this carries an indication that their previous disbelief will not harm them nor diminish their rewards.

﴿Gardens of perpetual residence (jannat 'adn)﴾ is a substitution (badal al-ba'd, partial substitution) for "Paradise," since it comprises them. Alternatively, it is in the accusative as an expression of praise (al-mad'h). It is also read in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject. ﴿'Adn﴾ is treated as a proper noun because it is the thing added to (al-mudaf ilayhi) in the sense of a proper name, or it is a proper name for "residence" (al-'adn bi-ma'na al-iqamah), like Burrah. For this reason it is valid to describe what is annexed to it by the phrase ﴿which the Most Merciful has promised to His servants in the unseen﴾, meaning He promised them while they are absent from it, or while they are absent from it (the gardens), or He promised them for their faith in the unseen.

﴿Indeed He﴾ i.e., Allah. ﴿His promise﴾ which is Paradise. ﴿is ever fulfilled (ma'tiyyan)﴾ its people will come to it, those promised to them, without doubt. It is said that it derives from "ata ilayhi ihsanan," meaning an accomplished, fulfilled favor.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 19, verse 62:

﴿They hear therein no idle talk﴾: superfluous speech. ﴿except "peace"﴾. But they hear a speech by which they are safe from fault and blame, or it is the angels' greeting of peace to them, or some of them greeting others, as a disconnected exception (*istithna' munqati'*, an exception whose excepted item is not of the same kind as what precedes it). Or, if the meaning of greeting is considered idle talk, then they hear no idle talk other than it, as in the poet's words:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords, with them, are notched from the clashing of the battalions."

Or its meaning is the supplication for safety, and the people of Paradise have no need of it, so it is, outwardly, of the category of idle talk, but its benefit is honour.

﴿And they will have their provision therein morning and evening﴾: in the manner of those who live in luxury, and a balance between asceticism and desire. It has also been said that what is meant is the constancy and abundance of the provision.

This is the Qur'an, surah 19, verse 63: "That is the Garden which We cause to inherit of Our servants whoever was godfearing (taqiyyan)."

We preserve it for them as the fruit of their piety, just as an heir is left the property of the one who bequeathed it. Inheritance (al-wirathah) is the strongest expression used for ownership and entitlement, in that it is not followed by cancellation or reclaiming, and is not nullified by refusal or relinquishment.

It has also been said: the godfearing inherit from the Garden the dwellings that were meant for the people of the Fire had they obeyed, as an increase in their honour. And it is related from Ya'qub that the verb is read as nuwarrithu with doubling (tashdid) of the ra'.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 64:

﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord.﴾ This is a report of the words of Jibril, upon him be peace, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was slow to receive revelation (ﷺ). This was when he was asked about the story of the People of the Cave, Dhu al-Qarnayn, and the Spirit, and he did not know how to answer. He hoped that revelation would come to him concerning it, but it was delayed for him fifteen days, and it is said forty days, until the polytheists said, "His Lord has bid him farewell and forsaken him." Then it descended with the explanation of that.

Al-tanazzul (descending) is descending gradually and by degrees, since it is the reflexive form (mutawaʿ) of nazala. It may also be used in the general sense of descending, just as nazala is used in the sense of anzala (to cause to descend). The meaning is: "We do not descend at one time after another except by the command of Allah, in accordance with what His wisdom requires." It is also read as «وَما يَتَنَزَّلُ» with the yaa, the pronoun referring to the revelation.

﴿To Him belongs what is before us, what is behind us, and what is between that﴾: this is the place and the times in which we are; we do not move from place to place, nor descend in one time rather than another, except by His command and His will.

﴿And your Lord was not forgetful﴾: abandoning you. Whatever the reason for the absence of descent, it was only because the command for it had not been given. That was not due to Allah abandoning you or bidding you farewell, as the disbelievers claimed; rather it was for a wisdom He saw in it.

It is also said that the beginning of the verse is a report of the words of the righteous (al-muttaqun) when they enter Paradise. The meaning is: "We do not enter Paradise except by the command of Allah and His grace, and He is the Owner of all affairs, past, anticipated and present. So what we have found and what we find of His grace and bounty..." His saying ﴿And your Lord was not forgetful﴾ is an affirmation from Allah of their words, meaning: "Your Lord was not forgetful of the deeds of those who labored, nor of the reward He promised them for them." And His saying:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 65:

﴿The Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ is an explanation of the impossibility of forgetfulness on His part, and it is either an omitted predicate (khabar) or a substitute (badal) for ﴿your Lord﴾. ﴿So worship Him and be steadfast in His worship﴾ is an address to the Messenger ﷺ, consequent upon what precedes it, meaning: since you have come to know your Lord, that it is not fitting for Him to forget you, or [since you have come to know] the deeds of the workers, then devote yourself to His worship and be steadfast in it, and do not be disturbed by the delay of revelation or the mockery of the disbelievers. It is construed with the preposition lam (li-) only because it includes the sense of persistence in worship amid the hardships and difficulties that befall one, like your saying to the warrior: "Stand firm against your opponent" (isṭabir li-qarnika). ﴿Do you know of anyone named with Him?﴾ meaning, a counterpart worthy of being called a god, or anyone called Allah. For the polytheists, even if they named an idol a god, they never named it Allah at all. This is because His oneness (aḥadiyyah) is manifest, and His Essence is exalted above likeness, such that it does not admit of confusion or obstinate denial. This is an affirmation of the matter.

That is: if it is established that there is no one like Him and no one other than Him deserves worship, then there is no alternative to submitting to His command, occupying oneself with His worship, and being steadfast in its hardships.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 66–67:

﴿And man says⦆ What is meant by it is the entire species (jins), for what is said is said among them even if not all of them say it, just as your saying: "The sons of so-and-so killed so-and-so," while the killer is one of them. Or it refers to a specific known group of them, who are the disbelievers, or Ubayy ibn Khalaf, for he took decayed bones, crumbled them, and said: "Muhammad claims that we will be resurrected after we die." ﴿When I am dead, shall I indeed be brought forth alive?﴾ from the earth, or from the state of death. The placing of the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) before the interrogative particle of denial (harf al-inkar) is because what is denied is the existence of what follows death at the time of life. Its accusative (intisab) is governed by a verb indicated by ﴿brought forth﴾, not by the phrase itself, for what comes after the lam (of emphasis) does not govern what precedes it. Here the lam is purely for emphasis (li'l-tawkid), stripped of the meaning of the present tense, just as the hamza and lam were made purely for compensation in "Ya Allah," so its combination with the particle of the future (harf al-istiqbal) is permissible. It is narrated from Ibn Dhakwan that he read ﴿idha ma mittu﴾ with a single kasra-marked hamza, as a statement of fact.

﴿Does not man remember⦆ It is coordinated (ʿutifa) upon "says" (yaqulu). The interposition of the hamza of denial between it and the conjunction, although the original order is for it to precede both, serves to indicate that what is denied in itself is the coordinated element, and that the element coordinated upon arises from it. For if he were to remember and reflect:

﴿That We created him before, when he was nothing﴾ but was pure non-existence, he would not say that, for the re-assembly of materials after dispersal and the bringing into being of the same accidents that were in them is more wondrous. Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim, and Qalun from Yaʿqub read (yadhdhakaru) from the remembrance (dhikr) that means reflection (tafakkur). It has also been read as "yatadhakkaru" according to the original form.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 19, verse 68:

﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them﴾. He swore by His name, the Exalted, joined to His Prophet, to confirm the matter and to magnify the status of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿and the devils﴾. It is either conjoined (*'uṭifa*) or in the accusative of accompaniment (*maf'ūl ma'ahu*). This is based on what is related: that the disbelievers will be gathered with their companions among the devils who misled them, each with his devil, in a chain. Although this applies specifically to them, it is permissible to attribute it to the whole category (of jinn and humans), for when they are gathered, with the disbelievers among them joined to the devils, they have all been gathered together with them.

﴿Then We will surely bring them forth around Hell﴾, so that the blessed may see what Allah has saved them from, and thus increase in joy and delight, and so that the wretched may receive what they stored up for their return as a punishment, and increase in rage at the return of the blessed away from them to the abode of reward, and at their gloating over them.

﴿kneeling﴾: on their knees, because of the terror of the scene they face. Or, because it is one of the consequences of standing for judgment before being conveyed to reward and punishment, and the people of the place of standing are kneeling, as in His saying, ﴿And you will see every nation kneeling﴾, in accordance with the customary posture in places of disputation. If by "the human" is meant the disbelievers, then perhaps they will be driven kneeling from the place of standing to the edge of Hell, as a humiliation for them, or because of their inability to stand due to the severity that has overtaken them.

Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī and Ḥafṣ read (*jithiyyan*) with a kasra on the *jīm*.

﴿Then We will surely draw out from every sect﴾: from every nation that adopted a religion (shāʿat dīnan). ﴿Which of them is most obstinate against the Most Merciful in rebellion?﴾ Whoever was most disobedient and most insolent among them, so We will cast them into it. Mentioning "the most" (al-ashadd) is an indication that He, exalted is He, pardons many of the people of disobedience. Even if this is restricted to the disbelievers, the meaning is that He distinguishes their groups, the most insolent from the most insolent, and casts them into the Fire in order, or He causes each to enter its own tier (ṭabaqa) that suits it. ﴿Which of them﴾ (ayyuhum) is indeclinable (mabnī) on the ḍamma according to Sībawayh (the grammarian), because its basic status is to be indeclinable like the other relative words (mawṣūlāt). However, it has been made declinable (aʿrib), by analogy with (kull) and (baʿḍ), because of the obligation of annexation (lazūm al-iḍāfa). When the first part of its relative clause is omitted, its deficiency increases, and so it returns to its proper status as accusative in place (manṣūb al-maḥall) by ﴿We will surely draw out﴾ (nanziʿanna). For this reason it has been read in the accusative. According to others, it is in the nominative, either as the subject (mubtadaʾ) with an interrogative sense (istifhāmī), and its predicate is ﴿most﴾ (ashaddu), and the clause is a reported question (maḥkiyya). The sense of the sentence is: "We will surely draw out from every sect those of whom it is said, 'Which of them is the most?'" Or it is suspended (muʿallaq) from ﴿We will surely draw out﴾, since it contains the meaning of distinction (tamyīz), which is necessary for knowledge. Or it is a new independent clause (mustaʾnafa), and the verb governs ﴿from every sect﴾, either with the addition of min (ziyādat min) or with the sense of "We will surely draw out some of every sect." It may also be governed by "sect" (shīʿa), because it means "partisanship" (tashayyuʿ), and ʿalā here is explanatory (lil-bayān), or it is connected to the imperative verb (uf'al). The same applies to the bāʾ in His saying:

﴿Then indeed We know best those who are most deserving of it, to be burned therein﴾ (ṣiliyyan). That is: indeed We know best those who most deserve to be burned (al-ṣilī), or their burning is most deserved for the Fire. They are the ones who are drawn out. It is also permissible that by them and by the most insolent among them (ashaddihim ʿitiyyan) is meant the leaders of the sects, since their punishment is doubled for their own misguidance and their misguiding of others. Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafṣ read ﴿ṣiliyyan﴾ with a kasra on the ṣād.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 71–72:

﴿And there is none of you﴾: "Minkum" (of you) here is not addressed to the human being, and this is supported by the reading "wa-inna minhum" (and indeed of them). ﴿but he will pass over it﴾: meaning, but he will reach it and be present close to it, which the believers pass by while it is extinguished, while it collapses upon others.

It is related on the authority of Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, that he (ﷺ) was asked about it and said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, some of them will say to others: 'Did not our Lord promise us that we would pass over the Fire?' It will be said to them: 'You have passed over it, and it is extinguished.'"

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Those will be kept far from it﴾, the meaning is far from its punishment. It has been said that their "coming upon" it is passing over the Sirat, for it is stretched over it. ﴿It was a decree decreed by your Lord﴾: their coming upon it was a binding obligation which Allah imposed upon Himself and decreed, by promising it as a promise that cannot be broken. It has also been said that He swore an oath concerning it.

﴿Then We will deliver those who were righteous﴾: so they will be driven to Paradise. Al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read ﴿nunajji﴾ with a light pronunciation (takhfif), and it has been read "thamma" with a fatha on the tha', meaning "there" (hunaka). ﴿And We will leave the wrongdoers therein, on their knees﴾: collapsing with them as they were, and this is evidence that what is meant by "coming upon" is kneeling around it, and that the believers separate from the sinners toward Paradise after their kneeling, while the sinners remain therein collapsed in their states.

﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them﴾, well arranged in their wording and explicit in their meanings, either through themselves or through the explanation of the Messenger (ﷺ), or manifestly inimitable. ﴿Those who disbelieved said to those who believed﴾, for their sake or in their company. ﴿Which of the two groups﴾, the believers or the disbelievers, ﴿is better in station﴾, in place of standing or location. Ibn Kathir read it with a *ḍamma* (maqāman), meaning a place of residence and dwelling. ﴿And better in assembly﴾, in gathering and congregation. The meaning is that when they heard the clear verses and were unable to counter them or to find a flaw in them (*al-dakhl ʿalayhā*), they began to boast of the worldly fortunes they possessed, and to argue from the increase of their share of them that they had superiority and a good standing before God Most High. This was because their outlook was limited to outward circumstances and their knowledge extended only to the apparent side of the worldly life. So He refuted them in this too, together with a threat, by refutation through His saying:

﴿And how many generations before them did We destroy, who were better in furnishings and appearance.﴾ *Kam* (how many) is the object of ﴿destroyed﴾, and ﴿from a generation﴾ is its specification (*bayan*). The people of each age were called a *qarn* (generation), meaning the front of an animal's horn (*qarn al-dabba*), because it is the front of the animal, since it precedes those who come after it. ﴿Who were better﴾ is an adjective of *kam*. ﴿Furnishings (athath)﴾ is a *tamyiz* (specification) of the relation, and it means household goods. It is said that it refers to what is new of them, while *al-kharthi* refers to what is worn out. *Al-riy'* means appearance, and it is a form derived from seeing (*al-ru'ya*), applied to what is seen, like *al-tahn* (grinding) and *al-khubz* (baking). Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read *riyyan*, either by changing the hamza and assimilating it, or as deriving from *al-riyy*, which is abundance of blessing. Abu Bakr read *riyiyan* by the change. It was also read *riyan* with the hamza dropped, and *ziyyan* from *al-zayy*, which is gathering. (p-18)

These are gathered beauties. Then he explained that their being given enjoyment is a gradual lure (*istidraj*) and not an honour, and that the measure of superiority and inferiority is what will be in the Hereafter, by his saying:

﴿Say: Whoever is in error, let the Most Merciful extend for him an extension﴾. So He extends him, grants him respite, and lets him live long and enjoy his life. He expressed it in the form of a command to indicate that granting him respite is something that should be done as a gradual drawing toward ruin (istidraj) and a cutting off of his excuses, like His saying: ﴿We only give them respite that they may increase in sin﴾, and His saying: ﴿Did We not give you life long enough that whoever would remember might remember therein?﴾. ﴿Until, when they see what they are promised﴾ is the end point of the extension. It has been said that the end point is the saying of those who disbelieved to those who believed, i.e., they said: "Which of the two groups is better?" until, when they see what they are promised. ﴿Either the punishment or the Hour﴾ is a specification of what is promised: it is either the punishment in this world, which is the victory of the Muslims over them and their being punished by them through killing and captivity, or it is the Day of Resurrection and what they will suffer therein of disgrace and torment. ﴿Then they will know who is worse in position﴾ of the two groups, by witnessing the matter contrary to what they had estimated, and what they were given to enjoy turns into abandonment and a burden upon them. This is the answer to the condition, and the sentence is narrated after the word حتى (ḥattā, "until"), which makes it a reported clause. ﴿And weaker in soldiers﴾ means weaker in group and helpers. He paired it with ﴿better in assembly﴾, since the goodness of an assembly lies in the gathering of the people's faces and notables and the manifestation of their strength and support.

﴿And Allah increases in guidance those who are guided﴾. This is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the reported conditional sentence (*sharṭiyya*, a sentence of the form "if... then...") that follows "speech" (*qawl*). It is as if, having made clear that the respite and provision of life in this world given to the disbelievers is not due to their merit, He wished to make clear that the scant share of the believer in it is not due to his deficiency, but because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, intends for him what is better for him and a recompense in place of it. It has also been said that it is conjoined to ﴿so let the Most Merciful extend him a extension﴾, because it carries the meaning of a statement, as if it were said: whoever is in error, Allah increases him in his error, and He increases in guidance the one who is his counterpart.

﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾: these are the acts of obedience whose benefit endures forever (*abad al-abad*). Included in them are what has been said to be the five prayers, and the sayings "Glory be to Allah," "Praise be to Allah," "There is no god but Allah," and "Allah is the Greatest."

﴿are better in the sight of your Lord as reward﴾: they are more beneficial than what the disbelievers have been provided with of blessings that are deficient and perishable, in which they take pride, especially since their outcome is lasting bliss, whereas the outcome of those blessings is regret and everlasting punishment, as He indicated by His saying: ﴿and better in return﴾. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verses 77–78:

﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs and said, "I will surely be given wealth and children"?﴾ It was revealed concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il. Khabbab had a claim against him for money, so he demanded payment, and he said to him: "No, not until you disbelieve in Muhammad." He said: "No, by Allah, I will not disbelieve in Muhammad, while alive or dead, nor when you are resurrected." When sight (ru'yah) was the strongest basis of reporting, the expression ara'ayta ("have you seen") was used in the sense of "tell me." The fa' (فاء) retains its original function of sequence (التعقيب, ta'qib), and the meaning is: "Tell the story of this disbeliever following the account of those [people]." **Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 19, verses 81–82:**

﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah that they may be for them a source of might.﴾ [They took them] so that they might gain strength through them, since they would be for them a means of access to Allah and intercessors with Him.

﴿No!﴾ This is a rebuke and a denial of their seeking might through them. ﴿They will deny their worship of them.﴾ The gods will disown their worship, and they will say, "You did not worship us," in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed.﴾ Or the disbelievers, because of the evil outcome, will deny that they worshipped them, in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then their trial will be only that they say, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾

﴿And they will be opposed to them﴾ [or: "will be a source of opposition to them"]. This supports the first interpretation if the word "opposition" (ḍidd) is understood as the opposite of might, meaning they will be a source of humiliation for them. Or it may be understood as their opposite, in the sense that they will be a means of aiding their punishment, by their fires being kindled with them. Or the waw (in "they will be") may be taken as referring to the disbelievers, meaning they will become disbelievers in them after having worshipped them. The singular form (ḍidd) is used because of the unity of the meaning by which they oppose one another, for they are, in this respect, like one thing. A parallel to this is his saying, upon him be blessings and peace (ﷺ): "They are a single hand against whoever is other than them."

It has been recited as *kullan* (كُلًّا) with tanwin, by converting the alif into a nun in pause, similar to the conversion of the alif of extension in the verse:

*"Lessen the blame, O reproacher, and the rebuke."*

Or, according to the meaning of this entire opinion, it is *kalla* and *kullan* with an implied verb whose meaning is explained by what follows it, that is: "They will deny"; ﴿No! They will deny their worship of them.﴾

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verses 83–84:

﴿Have you not seen that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers?﴾ That is, by empowering them over them, or by assigning to them companions (qurana'). ﴿They incite them with a determined incitement.﴾ They stir them up and urge them towards sins through embellishments (taswilat) and by making desires seem attractive (tahbib al-shahawat). The purpose is to express the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ wonder at the sayings of the disbelievers, their persistence in error (al-ghayy), and their obstinacy in disbelief after the truth has become clear, as the preceding verses have declared.

﴿So do not hasten against them﴾ for them to perish, so that you and the believers may be relieved of their evils and the earth may be purified of their corruption. ﴿Indeed, We are counting out for them﴾ the days of their terms (ayyam ajalihim). ﴿A specific count.﴾ The meaning is: do not hasten their destruction, for there remain for them only limited days and counted breaths.(p-20)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 85:

﴿On the Day We shall gather the God-fearing﴾ (nahshuru al-muttaqin), i.e., we shall assemble them. ﴿to the Most Merciful﴾ (ila al-Rahman), i.e., to their Lord, who overwhelmed them with His mercy. The choice of this name (al-Rahman) in this surah has significance, and perhaps it is because the thrust of this discourse in it is to enumerate His great blessings and to describe the condition of those who give thanks for them and of those who disbelieve in them. ﴿as a delegation﴾ (wafdan), i.e., coming to Him as envoys come before kings, awaiting their honor and bounty.

We drive the guilty ones (al-mujrimin) like cattle are driven, ﴿to Hell, in a thirsty state﴾, for one who comes to water comes only out of thirst, or like the animals that come to water.

﴿They will not possess intercession﴾: the pronoun in it refers to the servants (al-'ibad), which is indicated by the mention of the two categories, and it is the governing element (al-nasib) of "the Day." ﴿Except for one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾: except one who adorns himself with what makes him ready and qualifies him to intercede for the sinners, namely faith and righteous deeds, in accordance with what God the Exalted has promised; or, except one who has obtained from God a permission for it, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿On that Day intercession will not benefit, except for one whom the Most Merciful has permitted﴾. It derives from their saying: "The commander made a covenant (ahida) with so-and-so to do such-and-such," when he commanded him to do it. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the guilty ones, and the meaning is: they will not possess intercession on their behalf, except for one who has taken with the Most Merciful a covenant by which he prepares himself that He intercede for him through Islam.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verses 88–90:

﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken to Himself a son."﴾ The pronoun (al-damir) admits of both interpretations, because this statement, being something said among people, may be attributed to them.

﴿Indeed, you have produced a thing monstrous (iddan)﴾ This is an iltifat (shift in grammatical person) for the sake of intensifying the censure and emphasizing their audacity against Allah, the Exalted. Idd, with fatha or kasra, means the great and the abhorrent; idda means severity and the utmost of a matter. Adanī al-amr means "the matter weighed heavily upon me and became grievous to me."

﴿The heavens are almost torn apart﴾ Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read "takadu" with the ya' (yakadu). ﴿from it﴾ meaning they split repeatedly, one time after another. Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, Abu Bakr and Ya'qub read "yanfatirna." The first (yatafattarna) is more intensive, because the tafa''ul form is the intransitive counterpart of fa'ala, while the infi'al form is the intransitive counterpart of fu'ila; and because the basic sense of the tafa''ul form is effort and exertion. ﴿And the earth is split open and the mountains collapse in ruin﴾ They are crushed to ruin (hadd), or they are in a state of being crushed, or because they are crushed, i.e., broken into pieces. This is a confirmation of its being monstrous (iddan). The meaning is that the horror and enormity of this utterance is such that, were it given a perceptible form, these great bodies could not bear it and would crumble from its intensity. Or, its atrocity is a cause of the wrath of Allah, such that were it not for His forbearance the world would be ruined and its foundations scattered in anger against the one who uttered it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verses 96–97:

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—the Most Merciful will bring about for them affection.﴾ He will create for them affection in hearts, without any effort on their part to seek its causes,

and from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "When Allah loves a servant, He says to Jibril (Gabriel), 'I love so-and-so, so love him.' Then Jibril loves him, and then he calls out among the inhabitants of the heavens: 'Indeed Allah loves so-and-so, so love him.' Then the inhabitants of the heavens love him. Then love is placed for him on the earth."

The sin (in sayaj'alu, "He will bring about") may be [used] because the surah is Meccan, and they were despised at that time among the disbelievers, so He promised them this when Islam would spread; or because the promise is [fulfilled] on the Day of Resurrection, when their good deeds are displayed before the witnesses, and "what is in their breasts of rancor" is removed.

﴿So We have only made it easy in your tongue﴾ by sending it down in your language. The ba' (in bilisanika, "in your tongue") is in the sense of 'ala (upon), or it retains its original sense, because yassarnahu ("We made it easy") includes the meaning of anzalnahu ("We sent it down"), i.e., We sent it down in your language. ﴿That you may give glad tidings thereby to the God-fearing﴾, those who are heading toward taqwa (God-consciousness). ﴿And warn thereby a people most contentious﴾, those fierce in dispute, engaging in every kind of contention; i.e., [they are] split from the disputation due to the extreme obstinacy in them. So give glad tidings with it and warn.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 19, verse 98:

﴿And how many generations have We destroyed before them?﴾ This is a warning to the disbelievers and an encouragement to the Messenger (ﷺ) in warning them. ﴿Do you perceive any of them, or hear from them any faint sound?﴾ That is, do you sense any of them and see him? ﴿Or hear from them any faint sound (*rikzan*)?﴾ It is also recited as ﴿tasma'u﴾ (*tusmi'u*, "you cause to hear"), in the variant (*qira'ah*) reading. *Al-rikz* is a faint sound. The root *r-k-z* fundamentally denotes concealment, hence *rikz al-rumh* ("the spear's *rikz*"), when its tip is buried in the ground, and *al-rikaz* is buried wealth.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah Maryam will be given ten good deeds for each person who denied Zakariyya and affirmed him, and Yahya, Maryam, Isa, and the rest of the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, who are mentioned in it, and for each person who called upon Allah in this world, and for each person who did not call upon Allah."
